item.title: Grassroots official leads village on path to rural revitalization
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23
Zhong Baijun (R) learns about production at a village collective company in Xijidang Village, Zhewang Town of Lianyungang City, east China's Jiangsu Province, Aug. 19, 2026. Zhong Baijun, Party secretary of Xijidang Village and head of the village committee, has spent 28 years serving his hometown in Zhewang Town of Lianyungang City, east China's Jiangsu Province. When he returned to the village to take up his post in 1998, the village collective had no industries and was in debt. Most residents made a living from farming, and many younger villagers left home to seek work elsewhere. Looking for new ways to develop the local economy, Zhong and other village officials traveled to other areas to explore potential industries. Leveraging the village's coastal location and the relatively abundant stock of discarded fishing nets, they gradually developed a nylon pellet processing industry. The industry initially grew through small workshops. To restructure the sector, the village invested 120 million yuan (about 17.9 million U.S. dollars) in building a standardized industrial park and later developed a model that allowed residents to benefit from the industry's growth through shareholding, local employment and dividends. By 2025, Xijidang's total industrial output reached 2.5 billion yuan (about 372 million U.S. dollars). The industry also created jobs for more than 1,600 local residents. As the collective economy grew, the village put more resources into improving community well-being. It organized cultural and sports activities, as well as model-family award campaigns, giving residents more opportunities to take part in community events. Over the past 28 years, Zhong has witnessed the village's industries expand, employment opportunities increase and collective income rise. "We should put the people's concerns first," Zhong said. item.title: Regular Guangzhou-Shenzhen maritime cultural tourism route officially launched
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23
The cruise ship Da Wan Qu Yi Dun docks at the Nansha International Cruise Home Port in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province, Aug. 22, 2026. Named after the Greater Bay Area, known in Chinese as Da Wan Qu, the cruise ship Da Wan Qu Yi Dun departed from the Nansha International Cruise Home Port in Guangzhou on Saturday, marking the official launch of the regular Guangzhou-Shenzhen maritime cultural tourism route. Sailing past the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge, the Shenzhen-Zhongshan Link and 16 landmarks of the Greater Bay Area, the ship also provided visitors with diverse onboard experiences including performances themed on intangible cultural heritage and magic shows. item.title: Chinese teenagers flock to tech frontline to touch the future amid AI study-tour boom
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23
*To help children prepare for an AI-driven future, China unveiled an "AI Plus Education" initiative earlier this year, encouraging schools to take AI learning beyond the classroom through after-school programs and hands-on activities. *Moving beyond textbooks, students are flocking to tech giants, university labs and science centers, eager to get hands-on experience with cutting-edge AI technologies and see firsthand how the future is taking shape. *AI study camps are opening a new window onto how the technology is reshaping the world around them and how they can use it to make a difference. BEIJING, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- On a summer day, cheers erupted as clusters of children watched robots race across a soccer pitch, battling it out in playful matches, at a science center in Jiaxing, east China's Zhejiang Province. At a nearby workbench, nine-year-old Zhang Qihang was busy assembling a robot of his own. "Building robots is awesome! I can let my imagination run wild," he said, beaming with excitement. This was the scene at an artificial intelligence (AI) summer camp -- part of a new wave of study tours gaining traction across China. Moving beyond textbooks, students are flocking to tech giants, university labs and science centers, eager to get hands-on experience with cutting-edge AI technologies and see firsthand how the future is taking shape. AI STUDY-TOUR BOOM During this summer vacation, AI-themed study tours have begun to gain ground, with bookings surging 370 percent year on year, according to online travel platform Ctrip. To tap into the growing demand for AI-focused tech tourism, a travel agency based in Nanjing, east China's Jiangsu Province, began adding visits to technology companies to its trip programs last summer. "On our Shanghai-Hangzhou independent study tours, AI-related activities now account for more than 80 percent of the itinerary," founder Zhu Ping said. The boom is unfolding against the backdrop of China's broader AI boom, powered by a wave of homegrown models and applications. For a growing number of Chinese teenagers, AI tools such as DeepSeek, Kimi and Doubao are becoming familiar companions in their everyday lives. The number of AI enterprises in China had surpassed 6,000 last year, and the output value of the core AI industry was projected to exceed 1.2 trillion yuan (about 177 billion U.S. dollars) during the same period, representing a year-on-year increase of nearly 30 percent. Moreover, China was home to more than 140 humanoid robot developers in 2025, with shipments reaching 14,400 units -- accounting for 84.7 percent of the global market, according to an industry research report. To help children prepare for an AI-driven future, China unveiled an "AI Plus Education" initiative earlier this year, encouraging schools to take AI learning beyond the classroom through after-school programs and hands-on activities. The goal is to help students understand and use AI properly, while sparking curiosity, nurturing creativity and honing their critical-thinking and problem-solving skills. Today, the AI study-tour wave is sweeping through China's schools, as primary and secondary schools incorporate it into their educational programs. Parents are taking their children into the heart of the tech industry to see how AI transforms the real world. China's tech-tourism boom is also drawing international visitors keen to get a close-up look at the innovation behind "Made in China." Since opening in Shanghai in May, Unitree Robotics's first embodied intelligence experience store in Asia has attracted many foreign visitors. Victoria, from Denmark, visited the store last month. "I've seen some of the dancing videos, but it's really cool to see them in real life," she said, viewing the development of AI and robotics in China as "revolutionary, new and exciting." FROM AI USERS TO AI CREATORS Today's children are growing up as AI natives, already fluent in AI tools. But AI study camps are opening a new window onto how the technology is reshaping the world around them and how they can use it to make a difference. For Liang Yiduo, a Beijing middle school student, an AI summer camp run by internet giant NetEase offered a fresh perspective on the AI technology he thought he already knew. "I realized that large language models aren't just chatbots or simple tools," he said. "They can be assistants that work alongside you and help you create things tailored to your needs, like 'claws.'" "The goal of the study camp is to help children move from simply using AI to understanding it, creating with it and even building their own AI agents," said Wang Lijin, director and founder of Beijing Venus Future Education Consulting Center, which assists NetEase in running its study camps. Some study tour organizers design programs around students' interests and abilities, aiming to spark curiosity and encourage deeper thinking. Shanghai Qingbao Robot Co., Ltd., for example, offers students who enjoy building things the chance to assemble robotic arms and explore the mechanics of shoulder and neck structures. It also gives students a comparative look at the robotics and AI industries in China, the US, Europe and Japan, helping them gain a more balanced understanding of China's strengths and shortcomings. Wang Lei, the company's chairman, believes that study tours can greatly broaden students' horizons in science and innovation. "Through immersive study tours, students start thinking for themselves about how robotics can be applied to everyday life, from unmanned retail to automated pharmacies," he said. Some students are taking it a step further, learning to spot real-world problems and use AI to develop solutions. In the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, a group of students spent six days in a camp turning ideas into an AI-powered product. "I've realized that learning AI isn't about showing off what I can do with it, but about using it to solve real problems for others," said one team member. "I want to keep learning AI so I can help more people in the future." ■

item.title: Japan's two-front diplomatic push paves way for dangerous military expansion
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23
TOKYO, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- From Monday to Friday, Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi visited Australia and India, where he talked up strengthening Japan's so-called "counterstrike capabilities" and promoted exports of Japanese defense equipment. Analysts said that Japan's ruling authorities are aggressively pursuing a "diplomacy of military expansion," stepping up efforts on two fronts: expanding arms exports and broadening the scope of military activities. In doing so, they are steadily chipping away at the constraints on Japan by the postwar international order and legal frameworks. ONE AGENDA, TWO TRACKS According to analysts, the topics on the agenda of Koizumi's latest visits showed that Japan is accelerating its "remilitarization" push abroad along two tracks: expanding arms exports and broadening the scope of military activities. On arms exports, the administration of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has doubled down on efforts to market Japanese weapons and defense equipment overseas since it revised the "three principles on transfer of defense equipment and technology" and their implementation guidelines in April, lifting restrictions on exports of lethal weapons. Recently, it has been actively advancing the transfer of Japan's Abukuma-class destroyers to the Philippines. During his latest visits, Koizumi also sought to facilitate exports of the country's upgraded Mogami-class frigates to Australia, and the transfer of Unicorn communication antennas, which are installed on Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force destroyers, to India. Experts pointed out that the Takaichi administration's push to expand arms exports is not merely aimed at opening up markets for the domestic defense industry. It also seeks to forge closer ties with arms-buying countries on weapons systems, maintenance support, and parts supply, thereby further strengthening Japan's military influence overseas. On military activities, the Takaichi administration has accelerated efforts to expand the Self-Defense Forces' operational presence abroad, including sending a large contingent of combat personnel to the Philippines for joint military drills for the first time. During his trip to Australia, Koizumi reached a 10-year agreement with Australia, which will allow the Self-Defense Forces to use test sites in Australia to conduct test launches of long-range missiles to bolster so-called "counterstrike capabilities." Meanwhile, Japan and India also agreed to further deepen cooperation in joint exercises, with Japan Air Self-Defense Force fighter aircraft set to, for the first time, participate in a bilateral air force exercise in India scheduled for this year. Analysts said that the Japan-Australia agreement on long-range missile test-firing by the Self-Defense Forces on Australian soil signals a shift toward more sustained and institutionalized Japanese military activity in Australia. Japan's bilateral air force exercise with India, meanwhile, will mark another "dangerous first." Japan's push to deepen cooperation with relevant countries in maintenance, logistics, weapons development and other areas is, in effect, an attempt to extend its "strategic depth" and military capabilities beyond its borders, a move toward military expansion that runs counter to the principle of "exclusively defense-oriented policy." A "HIGHLY DANGEROUS" PATH OF MILITARY EXPANSION Since Takaichi took office, military and security issues have assumed an increasingly prominent place in Japan's diplomacy. While Koizumi was making his latest overseas visits, Takayuki Kobayashi, policy chief of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, traveled to three Pacific island countries, primarily seeking so-called "security cooperation." In media interviews, Kobayashi also played up the alleged growing political and economic influence of a "particular country" in the Pacific island nations. Analysts said these remarks amounted to inciting bloc confrontation. Whether through expanding arms exports, broadening the scope of military activities, or reinforcing "bloc-based security," the Takaichi government's diplomatic moves are all paving the way for its military buildup and rearmament. These moves undermine the postwar international order and violate Japan's domestic legal framework, including its pacifist Constitution, posing a serious threat to regional peace and stability. Tessa Morris-Suzuki, professor emerita of Japanese history at the Australian National University, wrote in an article that Takaichi's desire to remove the peace clause from the Japanese Constitution is something to worry about. Japanese experts also pointed out that the Takaichi administration's exaggerated portrayal of the so-called "the most severe and complex security environment since the end of World War II" also represents a return to the dangerous militarist rhetoric. Veteran Japanese journalist and former NHK anchor Tomoyoshi Kimura said Japan once launched wars of aggression under pretexts such as "self-preservation" and "self-defense," packaging military expansion as safeguarding its "own security and national survival." Today, he added, the Japanese government is once again using the guise of "strengthening defense capabilities" to push military buildup, calling it "necessary for defense." But in essence, it is steadily marching down a "highly dangerous" path of military expansion. ■

item.title: East China's Anhui eyes on strategic planning to foster future industries
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-22
* In the first half of 2026, Anhui's high-tech manufacturing added value surged 44.6 percent year on year, with sectors like electronic information and automobiles contributing over 70 percent of industrial growth. * While supporting private tech companies through the full cycle, Anhui is also accelerating the commercialization of technologies derived from large scientific facilities. * In Anhui, long-term planning and funding at both provincial and municipal levels ensure differentiated competition, which prevents redundant construction and enables cities to collaborate. HEFEI, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Along the "Quantum Avenue" in Hefei, provincial capital of Anhui, futuristic glass buildings house companies in quantum technology and digital services. Within the same vicinity sit facilities dedicated to voice recognition and deep-space exploration. Two decades ago, populous and less-developed Anhui in east China used to be an inland province with large labor outflow, but in the past years it has drawn a growing number of researchers and entrepreneurs who boast cutting-edge technologies. The province's long-term commitment to advanced technology has turned things around. In the first half of 2026, Anhui's high-tech manufacturing added value surged 44.6 percent year on year, with sectors like electronic information and automobiles contributing over 70 percent of industrial growth. CULTIVATING FUTURE GROWTH Early planning and sustained institutional support have advanced pioneering industries. Lu'an, a small city renowned for its tea production and picturesque mountains, is now home to China's first megawatt-class hydrogen energy demonstration station, which converts electricity into hydrogen and vice versa to regulate grid peaks and troughs. The station is expected to save around 1,091 tonnes of standard coal equivalent and reduce about 1,889 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually. Mingtian Hydrogen Energy Co., Ltd. is one of such operators. Since its founding in Lu'an in 2017, the company has proactively aligned itself with the provincial and municipal development framework. Backed by long-term policies, the company has partnered with the State Grid to establish the power station. For Wang Chaoyun, chairman of Mingtian Hydrogen Energy, the decision to set up in Lu'an was based on the city's diverse application scenarios for heavy freight and steel transport. "But what mattered more was that when some local officials mistook hydrogen energy for 'hydrogen bomb energy,' Anhui had already issued a clear hydrogen industry plan and set up dedicated industrial funds," Wang recalled. Wang and his team overcame numerous technical hurdles, at a time when China lacked a complete hydrogen supply chain. Some key components, such as air compressors, had to be imported at high costs and with lead times of at least four months. The city government stepped in to connect enterprises with research institutes. A physical sciences institute under the Chinese Academy of Sciences eventually developed a centrifugal air compressor, removing a critical bottleneck for local manufacturers. To mitigate the financial risks of heavy R&D investment, the city government partnered with insurers to provide partial compensation if the project failed. After the company moved into full-scale production, Lu'an pioneered hydrogen fuel cells in its public bus fleet, with about a quarter of the buses now hydrogen-powered. The move not only helped the company gain operational experience but also served as a strong commercial endorsement. Today, Mingtian Hydrogen Energy has built a complete industrial chain covering fuel cell manufacturing and hydrogen-electricity storage, and its hydrogen-powered marine systems have obtained certification from the China Classification Society. "Anhui embraces new thinking, new technologies and new industries. The government here has a long-term vision and the courage to break new ground and take responsibility," said Wang. FROM LAB TO MARKET While supporting private tech companies through the full cycle, Anhui is also accelerating the commercialization of technologies derived from large scientific facilities. These spinoffs not only serve the public but also generate economic returns that are reinvested into long-term R&D. At Hefei Ion Medical Center, a domestically developed superconducting proton therapy system is undergoing clinical preparations and is expected to treat patients this year. It grew directly out of core technologies accumulated during the development of the Experimental Advanced Superconducting Tokamak (EAST), dubbed China's "artificial sun," which aims to create nuclear fusion like the sun. These technologies include superconducting magnets, radiofrequency systems and ion sources. Compared with conventional radiotherapy, the proton system precisely targets tumors while significantly reducing radiation damage to surrounding vital organs. This drastically lowers long-term complications and improves patients' quality of life. This is far from unique. In Hefei, subway passengers pass through terahertz scanners, another innovation derived from the EAST fusion project. The technology outperforms conventional security devices by detecting prohibited objects previously overlooked, such as ceramic knives, liquid hazardous chemicals, and powdered drugs. For companies seeking business opportunities in big science spinoffs, the Anhui Innovation Hall offers a one-stop hub that showcases more than 2,700 high-level international achievements and provides transaction and matchmaking services. The Anhui Innovation Hall has trained over 5,100 "technology managers." With expertise in technology, industry and finance, these professionals offer end-to-end services from scouting to deal-making. The service network has facilitated the commercialization of more than 4,000 research results over the past six years. This incubator is adopting a more proactive approach. "We have regularly stationed our managers on campus at the University of Science and Technology of China to engage with research teams at the earliest stage, connecting their work with provincial funding and applications, turning breakthroughs into tangible outcomes," said Li Wenxin, deputy director of the hall. INVESTING IN CHAINS With Hefei's stake in ChangXin Memory Technologies, China's leading memory chipmaker now worth over one trillion yuan (about 140 billion U.S. dollars), Hefei is called China's boldest "venture capital city." But its investment does not aim to bet on individual companies for financial returns, but aims to extend and strengthen industrial chains based on regional strengths. In 2008, Hefei invested approximately 6 billion yuan in the sixth-generation production line of BOE Technology Group Co., Ltd. The move shored up a shortfall in local home appliance production and created China's first homegrown liquid crystal display supply. In 2020, it injected 7 billion yuan into NIO China, anchoring the electric vehicle maker's headquarters and R&D center locally and expanding its Anhui-based suppliers from about 60 to nearly 150. Through these anchor companies, Hefei has cultivated national-level strategic emerging industrial clusters in new display technology, integrated circuits and AI. Quantum information, fusion energy and deep-space exploration are now its next frontiers. Beyond Hefei, cities across Anhui are also nurturing their own signature industries. As of the first quarter of 2026, Anhui's first 10 provincial-level future-industry pilot zones had already generated over 93 billion yuan in total industrial-chain output. Bengbu City, leveraging its core competencies in integrated circuits and new materials, has achieved a breakthrough in brain-computer interface (BCI) technology. A local hospital can carry out clinical work for both semi-invasive BCI surgeries and non-invasive BCI systems, offering patients with paralysis a path to restored independence in daily living. "In Anhui, each city builds on its local strengths and supports leading enterprises to drive industrial chain development. Long-term planning and funding at both provincial and municipal levels ensure differentiated competition, which prevents redundant construction and enables cities to collaborate," said Cui Shihua, deputy director of the Bengbu high-tech zone's management committee. (Video reporter: Qu Yan; video editors: Zhang Yucheng and Liu Xiaorui)■

item.title: China activates Level-IV flood emergency response for Guangdong, Guangxi, Hainan
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-22
BEIJING, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Water Resources on Saturday activated a Level-IV emergency response to flooding in Guangdong, Guangxi and Hainan, as Typhoon Narra is forecast to bring torrential rains to southern China. From Aug. 22 to 24, Narra, the 19th typhoon of this year, will bring heavy to torrential rainfall across southern and western Guangxi, Guangdong and Hainan, with some areas expecting extremely heavy downpours, the ministry said. Water levels are forecast to rise in several rivers in Guangxi, Guangdong and Hainan. The Zuojiang and Mingjiang rivers, tributaries of the Yujiang River, as well as some small and medium-sized rivers in the rainstorm-hit areas may see floods above warning levels. The ministry has urged local water resources departments to closely monitor the typhoon's development, strengthen rain and river monitoring, forecasting, and early warning, while ensuring the scientific operation of water conservancy projects. It stressed the importance of preventing mountain torrents and small and medium-sized river floods, ensuring reservoir safety during the flood season, and implementing safety measures for tourists and construction workers. Authorities should dynamically update high-risk area catalogs, evacuate residents from hazardous areas in a timely manner, and make every effort to safeguard people's lives and property, the ministry added. Also on Saturday, the State Flood Control and Drought Relief Headquarters and the Ministry of Emergency Management jointly activated a Level-IV emergency response for typhoon and flood control in southeastern Fujian Province. China has a four-tier flood-control emergency response system, with Level I being the most severe. ■

item.title: Chinese customs official calls for more APEC efforts to remove trade barriers
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-22
DALIAN, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- APEC economies should step up efforts to eliminate trade barriers and take more concrete measures to address cross-border trade bottlenecks, so as to make supply chains in the Asia-Pacific region safer, more stable and more efficient, a Chinese customs official said on Saturday. "Security and facilitation are eternal themes of customs governance," Zhang Baofeng, deputy chief of the General Administration of Customs, said at the ongoing second plenary meeting of the 2026 APEC Sub-Committee on Customs Procedures (SCCP) in Dalian, northeast China's Liaoning Province. Amid growing fragmentation of global supply chains, adjusting rules and standards and strengthening supply chain resilience have never been more urgent, Zhang noted. He expressed hope that all parties will take the meeting as an opportunity to deepen alignment of rules and standards, strengthen coordination on risk management and supervision, reduce transaction costs, improve customs clearance efficiency, and provide businesses with a safer, more transparent and more predictable business environment. The Asia-Pacific region, home to one-third of the world's population, accounts for over 60 percent of the global economy and nearly half of global trade, serving as a key engine of global economic growth. China's trade with other APEC economies totaled 18 trillion yuan (about 2.65 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first seven months of this year, up 21 percent year on year, outpacing overall growth in China's foreign trade in goods and demonstrating strong potential for regional cooperation. During the meeting, participants observed smart devices, exchanged experience and ideas, and built consensus. China's customs shared the latest progress of the smart customs partnership program and held an exhibition showcasing achievements in smart customs development. Zhang also put forward a three-point proposal to further deepen APEC customs cooperation -- upholding true multilateralism and jointly building a new pattern of open and inclusive Asia-Pacific cooperation; riding the wave of the digital era and reshaping new paradigms of customs governance with technological innovation; balancing security and facilitation, and underpinning lasting prosperity in the Asia-Pacific region with a resilient and stable supply chain system. The meeting also approved an APEC customs cooperation document on promoting technology and innovation for trade security and facilitation. The APEC SCCP was established in 1994. China's customs holds the SCCP chairmanship for 2026. This meeting, following the first plenary in Guangzhou in February this year, featured in-depth discussions on cutting-edge topics such as artificial intelligence, smart customs and cross-border e-commerce. Over 100 delegates, including customs representatives from all 21 APEC economies and officials from relevant government departments, international organizations, and business communities, attended the meeting. ■

item.title: China's top anti-graft body vows higher standards, more concrete measures to advance its work
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-22
Li Xi, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and secretary of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI), addresses the sixth plenary session of the 20th CCDI of the CPC in Beijing, capital of China, Aug. 22, 2026. (Xinhua/Yue Yuewei) BEIJING, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- The sixth plenary session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) of the Communist Party of China (CPC) was held in Beijing on Saturday. Li Xi, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and secretary of the CCDI, addressed the session. The session called for steadfastly following the Chinese path to combat corruption and advance the high-quality development of discipline inspection and supervision work in the new era, with higher standards and more concrete measures. The session reviewed discipline inspection and supervision work in the first half of 2026 and made further arrangements to ensure the effective implementation of relevant tasks. It called for strengthening political oversight, deepening political inspections, strictly enforcing discipline in leadership transitions, unswervingly improving conduct, enforcing discipline and combating corruption, and continuing concentrated rectification of misconduct and corruption at the people's doorsteps, to ensure the high-quality completion of all tasks for the year. The session elected Zhao Shiyong deputy secretary of the CCDI, and Zhang Zhong deputy secretary of the CCDI and a member of its Standing Committee. ■

item.title: Chinese robotics fair draws crowds as industry brews innovation
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-22
BEIJING, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Unitree Robotics' blockbuster IPO, the bustling World Robot Conference (WRC), and the upcoming World Humanoid Robot Games, amount to a string of high-profile events which have combined to make this week a "super week" for Chinese robotics. Underpinning these events is a clear trend: China is swiftly becoming a global epicenter of robotics innovation, which is poised to reshape the way products are manufactured and the way people live. The numbers confirm China's significant rise in robotics. Data from the country's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology show that revenue of industrial enterprises above designated size in China's robotics sector had exceeded 300 billion yuan (about 44.24 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, with an average annual growth rate of more than 20 percent over the past five years. Also, a report by California-based research firm Smart Analytics Global indicates that global humanoid robot shipments totaled approximately 19,100 units in the first half of 2026, with Chinese-made units accounting for over 97 percent of the total. More broadly, exports of industrial robots increased 13.2 percent in the January-July period, while shipments of surgical robots surged 3.3-fold year on year in the first half of 2026. Robots, AI products and innovative drugs are three new drivers of China's export growth, according to Science and Technology Minister Yin Hejun. This momentum has played out at this year's WRC, which is being held in a southeastern technology hub in Beijing. On weekday mornings, traffic ground to a halt for kilometers around the WRC exhibition hall, forcing the organizers to issue daily "travel advisories," a task that speaks volumes about the sector's red-hot vitality in China. Inside the venue, crowds are so dense they rival the throngs at CES in Las Vegas. WRC exhibitors this year have topped 300, up 69 percent from 2025, with the event featuring over 3,000 products, and roughly 300 making their debuts. Additionally, many are powered by large AI models, cloud computing and big data. China's vast and sophisticated manufacturing sector is providing a massive testing ground for embodied AI technologies, which are now being deployed on a large scale in factories and training facilities. According to an industry research report, by June this year, China had launched over 70 training grounds for robots, with another 46 either under construction or in the planning pipeline. "This week's IPO is just the start of the journey," said Aron Kisdi, managing director of Autodiscovery and Unitree Robotics' U.K. distributor, at the company's WRC booth. Unitree Robotics, based in Hangzhou in east China, went public on China's A-share market on Wednesday, the same day the WRC opened, and its shares skyrocketed 629.44 percent to open at 1,100 yuan. "It signals that the time in the lab is nearing an end, and we're pushing robots into the real world," Kisdi explained. On the exhibition floor at the WRC, many booths are displaying robots operating in real-world work scenarios. A logistics robot sorts parcels at a rate of more than 1,000 items per hour, while nearby, a pair of dexterous robotic hands smoothly folds a cardboard sheet into a packaging box. At UBTECH's display zone, robots perform automated loading and unloading of automotive sheet metal parts with zero human oversight, building on earlier trials at several car plants. Chinese robotics firms have, notably, already put robots into factories to test their capability of doing more sophisticated jobs beyond just basic handling. Elsewhere at the show, automakers like Xiaomi feature their own humanoid robots, underscoring how industry demand is fueling robotics innovation. The bustling expo floor in Beijing also features robots designed for emotional companionship, housework, convenience-store retail and coffee brewing, which can tap into China's massive consumer market, the world's second-largest in terms of commodity consumption for more than 10 consecutive years. "Robots are no longer only about flashy concepts and specs. They're increasingly focused on tackling real-life challenges," said Ren Jingwei, a manager at Zhiyuan Research Institute in Hangzhou. Also, this year's WRC fair is no longer just for curious onlookers. Industry players up and down the supply chain are busy exchanging business cards and phone numbers there in bids to forge new partnerships. One noteworthy shift this year is the considerable presence of dexterous-hand sensor makers, joint module suppliers and chip manufacturers at the WRC. These component suppliers, once supporters behind finished robots, have now also taken center stage in their own niche sectors -- a sign that China's robotics industry is maturing into a more sophisticated ecosystem. Humanoid robots could spur investment across precision transmission, smart sensors, AI chips and intelligent software, generating a huge market from R&D to after-sales service, said Xu Xiaolan from the Chinese Institute of Electronics. To many attendees, Beijing's robot show points to an upcoming transformative change in the industry. The "ChatGPT moment" for embodied AI will come in two to three years under an optimistic outlook, or within five to ten years at the latest, said Wang Xingxing, Unitree Robotics founder and CEO, when speaking at a WRC forum. ■
